title: What will you be?
hookLine: consider what you'll be when death arrives (Meditations 12.7)

lines: A WILL FOR WHAT YOU LEAVE.
cards: People write wills about what they'll leave behind: the house, the savings, the watch for the grandson. A will rarely says who you hope to be by then.
Near the very end of his notebook, in a single sentence, Marcus comes at that second question. He doesn't ask what you'll own when death comes, or what you'll have achieved. He asks something harder.

teach.b: First, the sentence. Consider, Marcus writes, what condition you ought to be in, body and soul, when death overtakes you.

teach.h: SHORT LIFE, VAST TIME, FRAIL MATTER.
teach.b: Then think about how short life is, the vast gulf of time behind and ahead of it, and how fragile all matter is. Second, the shape of it. Notice the order.
First the person. Then the timeline: a short life set inside an enormous stretch of time. Then the material: everything made of stuff that breaks down.
He isn't trying to frighten himself. He's trying to see clearly, so that what matters stands out.
Third, why be and not have. Death will find you somewhere, doing something. Marcus doesn't ask where.
He asks what kind of person it will find. That moves the question from achievements to character. You can't control when; you can work on who.
Fourth, the week, looking back. Nine reminders. Four failures.
Remember them. No thief. Now, not later.
My own opinion. And now, what will I be.

teach.h: A WEEK OF SHAPING A PERSON.
teach.b: Each one was a way of shaping the person death would find: someone who answers offense with reasons, catches the mind's wrong turns, remembers good people, keeps hold of the choice, begins now, and trusts their own honest judgment.
Book twelve is drawing the notebook toward its close, and this is the question it hands you.

how: Some readers of the Meditations keep a few written words describing the person they hope to become, and reread them as a way of sorting what matters in an ordinary day.

o: the gap between who you are and who you want to be
the endless time before and after a short life
the distance between the emperor and his people

games.q: what will you be? — tap the pairs.
p: a short life in a vast gulf of time

s: Marcus asks what you will own when you die
he asks what condition, body and soul, death should find you in.
he sets the question beside the vastness of time before and after a life
the shortness of life, and the gulf of time behind and ahead.

games.q: you're Marcus, near the end of the notebook, thinking about your death. what do you ask?
o: what kind of person should death find me?
how can I put it off?
games.why: consider what you should be, in body and soul, when death overtakes you, he writes.

practice: Imagine, gently, a day many years from now, and ask who you'd like to be by then: not what you'd like to have, but who. Kind, patient, honest, brave; let two or three words come, and just hold them while you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Vast gulf. Marcus sets a short life against the vast gulf of time behind and ahead of it, and asks what you'll be when death comes. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: an age, a lifetime, a long stretch of time.

carryVoice: Your line: what will I be. Character is the one thing his question asks about. That's a week; rest well.
